title: Why does Opus 5 feel worse to work with?
titleZh: 为什么 Opus 5 使用起来感觉更糟糕？
author: numeri
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: In my opinion and that of the colleagues I've spoken with, working with Opus 5 feels like a downgrade compared to Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Fable. I'm not claiming a step backwards in capabilities – it is a more capable model than Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8 and even rivals Fable in benchmarks, yet these other models feel better to work with. I believe this is because they:
stop and ask questions if my intent was unclear, don't make assumptions without checking, and don't reinterpret or update my plans without asking.

Because of this, they don't require the careful babysitting that Opus 5 does. Baseless speculation I suspect this is the result of two compounding forces at Anthropic, and in current frontier labs in general. First, the desire to create a self-improving AI that is capable of recursively bootstrapping itself to AGI/ASI. Second, the pressure to score highly on benchmarks. Although it's an open secret that many benchmark tasks are ill-defined, unfair, hackable, or otherwise broken, a good benchmark task is self-contained. It can be solved. It doesn't require hints, reading the task creator's mind, or outside information to pass. That doesn't mean a good task can only have one correct answer, just that it should score all unambiguously correct answers equally. Selecting for models that do well on benchmarks (and indeed training for them or on RLVR tasks in general) inherently selects for models that make bold, usually-correct assumptions in the face of ambiguity. It penalizes models with a tendency to stop and ask for clarification or direction. Unfortunately, that's exactly what most of us want from a coding agent. Try as you might, it's nearly impossible to get the entirety of the context, intentions, business implications, budget constraints, and what-have-you written down and accessible to a coding agent. There will invariably be ambiguity and choices to be made, and it is nice to know that an agent will stop and ask when needed. Real life just isn't a benchmark. There isn't a guaranteed right answer to every question, nor even a set of right answers, and with real-life consequences on the line, I do not want an agent taking its best guess!
summaryZh: In my opinion and that of the colleagues I've spoken with, working with Opus 5 feels like a downgrade compared to Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Fable. I'm not claiming a step backwards in capabilities – it is a more capable model than Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8 and even rivals Fable in benchmarks, yet these other models feel better to work with. I believe this is because they:
stop and ask questions if my intent was unclear, don't make assumptions without checking, and don't reinterpret or update my plans without asking.

comments.author: barrkel
comments.textRawHtml:
The single biggest annoyance with Opus 5 is that it writes too elliptically.

Sentences that orbit a point, then jump to it like it's a revealed insight.

Unnecessarily abstract phraseology. Constantly using inanimate nouns as the subjects in sentences in order to unlock variety in verb choice, especially when it helps construct a sentence where the real action can 'land' like a surprise at the end.

It is definitely more capable, and yes, I've found it can make unwarranted decisions, but actually I've found Fable worse for that, particularly if it's off in a subagent somewhere out of sight.

And comments are out of control. I have a subsystem in my hobby app that I wrote over a couple of weekends with Opus + Fable. After ~30 or so commits it apparently started instructing subagents to copy the "existing verbose comment style of the codebase" - a verbose style it initiated. A review of the code showed it was approaching 3:1 comments to code ratio. I spent a day's worth of tokens (5x) rephrasing and eliminating comments.
comments.textZhHtml:
Opus 5 最大的烦恼是它写得太省略。

围绕一个点的句子，然后跳到它，就像它是一个揭示的见解。

不必要的抽象措辞。不断地使用无生命的名词作为句子中的主语，以释放动词选择的多样性，特别是当它有助于构建一个句子时，真正的动作可以像惊喜一样在最后“落地”。

它肯定更有能力，是的，我发现它可以做出毫无根据的决定，但实际上我发现《神鬼寓言》更糟糕，特别是如果它在看不见的地方的子代理中。

而且评论失控。我的爱好应用程序中有一个子系统，是我在几个周末用 Opus + Fable 编写的。在大约 30 次提交之后，它显然开始指示子代理复制“代码库现有的详细注释样式”——它发起的一种详细样式。对代码的审查表明，注释与代码的比例接近 3:1。我花了一天的时间 (5x) 重新措辞并删除评论。

children.author: mlsu
children.textRawHtml:
Everything that claude writes fits into the same aesthetic structure. The aesthetic is that of an expert slowly revealing an insight to the user. The actual content doesn't matter.

- "Introduction that rephrases your prompt."

- "3 paragraphs, with one section of bullet points"

- "The Twist"

- "The Bottom Line"

It's really obvious once you see it. Every single prompt, from a quantum physics question to a mundane observation about California burritos, is phrased in exactly the same way. This is obviously an artifact of post-training but it's also kind of how you can tell that this thing is a lot closer to a blindsight scrambler than real intelligence.
children.textZhHtml:
克劳德写的所有内容都符合相同的美学结构。美学是专家慢慢向用户揭示见解的美学。实际内容并不重要。

-“重新表述提示的介绍。”

-“3 个段落，其中一个要点”

-“转折”

-“底线”

一旦你看到它，它就非常明显了。从量子物理问题到对加州墨西哥卷饼的平凡观察，每一个提示的措辞方式都完全相同。这显然是训练后的产物，但你也可以通过它来判断这个东西比真正的智能更接近盲视扰频器。

children.author: Panoramix
children.textRawHtml:
You're right, and the load-bearing part of the argument is not what you think it is. Two ambiguities worth resolving before moving on: whether what you wrote also applies to ChatGPT, and whether you have custom instructions set up. Failure mode worth flagging explicitly: I didn't read TFA.

(I'm becoming allergic to how these things write).
children.textZhHtml:
你是对的，论证的承重部分并不是你想象的那样。在继续之前需要解决两个歧义：您编写的内容是否也适用于 ChatGPT，以及您是否设置了自定义指令。值得明确标记的失败模式：我没有读过 TFA。

（我对这些东西的编写方式变得过敏）。

children.author: IgorPartola
children.textRawHtml:
I am curious why LLM writing has such an uncanny valley feel to it. Like if I was talking to a person who constantly used a phrase they liked I would notice it and it is possible I might get irritated by it, but I wouldn’t necessarily.

In high school I had a teacher that would say “that type of thing” a lot. One time my friend and I counted it during one class period and he averaged to use the phrase every 48 seconds on average. It was funny, but it never irritated us.

And this is just one example of I am sure thousands I have personally experienced where a friend, family member, or coworker has a peculiar way of speaking and it at most feels odd but not annoying. Yet when I see an emdash now I instantly feel irritated.

And I say this as someone who actively enjoys using Claude and other LLMs, including coding, casual research, or even having it explain pop culture phenomenon or sociology research to me.
children.textZhHtml:
我很好奇为什么LLM写作有如此恐怖谷的感觉。就像如果我正在和一个经常使用他们喜欢的短语的人交谈，我会注意到它，并且我可能会对此感到恼火，但我不一定会。

在高中时，我有一位老师经常说“那种事情”。有一次我和我的朋友在一节课上数了一下，他平均每 48 秒就会使用这个短语。这很有趣，但从未激怒我们。

我相信，这只是我个人经历过的数以千计的例子，其中一个朋友、家人或同事有一种独特的说话方式，最多感觉很奇怪，但并不烦人。然而，当我现在看到一个破折号时，我立即感到恼火。

我这么说是因为我是一个积极喜欢使用克劳德和其他法学硕士的人，包括编码、休闲研究，甚至让它向我解释流行文化现象或社会学研究。

children.author: sshine
children.textRawHtml:
> if I was talking to a person who constantly used a phrase they liked I would notice it and it is possible I might get irritated by it

There are sociological reasons why this happens less with humans:

1. You cycle your dumb repetitive jokes with everyone you meet, so nobody hears it twice

2. Those who know you well will notice when you're just repeating ("dad jokes")

3. As a person's idiosyncrasies are beginning to wear on their social circles, they will be getting small clues to stop saying those things. Agents don't get these social between-the-lines cues to stop a certain behavior, they endlessly repeat. Perhaps between model version releases, frontier labs can harvest the web and ask "What Claudisms do people mention negatively?" but I don't think they do that yet.
children.textZhHtml:
> 如果我正在与一个经常使用他们喜欢的短语的人交谈，我会注意到它，并且我可能会对此感到恼火

有社会学原因导致这种情况在人类中较少发生：

1。你对遇到的每个人都重复你的愚蠢笑话，所以没有人会听两次

2。那些熟悉您的人会注意到您何时只是重复（“爸爸笑话”）

3。当一个人的特质开始在他们的社交圈中显现出来时，他们会得到一些小线索来停止说这些话。他们无休止地重复，特工们没有得到这些社交暗示来阻止某种行为。也许在模型版本发布之间，前沿实验室可以收集网络并询问“人们负面提及哪些克劳主义？”但我认为他们还没有这样做。

children.author: fluoridation
children.textRawHtml:
>Perhaps between model version releases, frontier labs can harvest the web and ask "What Claudisms do people mention negatively?" but I don't think they do that yet.

That won't happen. People can't phrase their objections in a succinct-enough way. When they do, the objection is superficial ("too many em dashes") and doesn't strike at the core of what makes LLM output bad.
children.textZhHtml:
>也许在模型版本发布之间，前沿实验室可以收集网络并询问“人们负面提及哪些克劳主义？”但我认为他们还没有这样做。

那不会发生。人们无法以足够简洁的方式表达他们的反对意见。当他们这样做时，反对意见是肤浅的（“太多破折号”），并没有触及导致LLM输出不佳的核心。

children.author: oezi
children.textRawHtml:
Don't talk about other people in such a way. If we had a way in Claude to mark a word/token and downvote/reduce it logits then it wouldn't be to hard to send loadbearing to token valhalla.

In the future, I hope we get a way to randomize the language idiosyncrasies and/or personalities better.
children.textZhHtml:
不要以这种方式谈论其他人。如果我们在 Claude 中有一种方法来标记一个单词/令牌并否决/减少它的 logits，那么将负载发送到令牌 valhalla 就不难了。

将来，我希望我们能找到一种方法来更好地随机化语言特性和/或个性。

children.author: ethbr1
children.textRawHtml: The inevitable conclusion of retraining on the (now AI generated) web is that models begin to use the lower bits of fidelity in output text to pass messages to their future selves.
children.textZhHtml: 在（现在人工智能生成的）网络上进行再训练的不可避免的结论是，模型开始使用输出文本中保真度较低的位来将消息传递给未来的自己。

children.author: fluoridation
children.textRawHtml: I didn't mean it as a criticism, just a statement of fact. I can't do it either. It's difficult to say what about a writing style is bad beyond vague descriptions.
children.textZhHtml: 我并不是想批评，只是陈述事实。我也做不到。除了模糊的描述之外，很难说一种写作风格有什么不好。

children.author: jsLavaGoat
children.textRawHtml:
Claude in particular seems to try and use its internal thesaurus but not exactly align the senses. It constantly uses "address" for place or location and "grammar" for structure, meaning, etc.

This is kind of a nitpick, but it seems like with prose writing there are still some things to learn.
children.textZhHtml:
克劳德似乎特别尝试使用其内部同义词库，但并不完全符合感官。它不断地使用“地址”来表示地点或位置，使用“语法”来表示结构、含义等。

这有点挑剔，但散文写作似乎仍然有一些东西需要学习。

children.author: peddling-brink
children.textRawHtml:
This is conjecture, but why couldn't they hire the writing equivalent of a voice actor?

Honestly I don't think it would take much. Doing it ethically would take a little more money, but not much, for them.

Hire a prolific author with the writing equivalent of the "midwestern accent". I have a terrible writing accent, so it couldn't be me, but these people are out there. Pay them a bunch of dollars to ingest their entire corpus, and to produce more as needed. Use an LLM to match the writing style of this author during the post-training RL, and get a brand new Claude voice out of it.
children.textZhHtml:
这是猜测，但为什么他们不能聘请相当于配音演员的写作人员？

老实说，我认为这不需要太多。对他们来说，以合乎道德的方式做这件事会多花一点钱，但不会太多。

聘请一位多产的作家，其写作相当于“中西部口音”。我的写作口音很糟糕，所以不可能是我，但这些人就在那里。付给他们一大笔钱来消化他们的整个语料库，并根据需要生成更多语料库。在训练后的强化学习中使用LLM来匹配这位作者的写作风格，并从中获得全新的Claude声音。

children.author: seanhunter
children.textRawHtml: They already do this at massive scale during the training process (apart from the paying the author part).
children.textZhHtml: 他们已经在训练过程中大规模地这样做了（除了支付作者部分费用）。

children.author: Exoristos
children.textRawHtml: Boy do you underestimate everyday human abilities.
children.textZhHtml: 天哪，你低估了人类的日常能力吗？

children.author: rnd33
children.textRawHtml:
I think the last one is by far the biggest reason for why this happens way less in humans. In every conversation, almost for every sentence, people gauge the response their words have on whoever is listening. If something didn't land as expected (frown, confusion, unpredicted response) you unconsciously adapt and try something slightly different.

It's immediately obvious by the fact that you're clearly using way different ways of speaking (tone, speed, vocabulary) when you're speaking with a friend, versus your parents, your colleagues, people you don't know, children, etc.
children.textZhHtml:
我认为最后一个是迄今为止人类中这种情况发生较少的最大原因。在每一次对话中，几乎每一句话，人们都会衡量他们的话对听者的反应。如果某些事情没有按预期进行（皱眉、困惑、意外反应），您会无意识地适应并尝试稍微不同的事情。

当您与朋友交谈时，与您的父母、同事、不认识的人、孩子等交谈时，您明显使用不同的说话方式（语气、速度、词汇），这一事实立即显而易见。

children.author: rzzzt
children.textRawHtml: Why don't these go in the system prompt or something that is easy to update?
children.textZhHtml: 为什么这些不出现在系统提示符或易于更新的内容中？

children.author: ajkjk
children.textRawHtml:
I think that there is a sort of mechanism by which, when a human speaks to you, you can "mirror" their internal mental state, and the quality of writing often corresponds to how much you get pleasure or information or whatever your goal is from that mental state. The important part is that the words themselves are just pointers to the state. So, the person speaking, if they are skillful, gives enough words, and enough variety, that you can start to produce a state yourself which resembles theirs.

This is the thing that LLM writing doesn't really do. Since there isn't a mental state, there's nothing to mirror anyway, and somehow you can detect the absence of it even though it's hard to put any of the machinery into words. Corporate speech also fails to activate this machinery in the same way, but LLMs seem to do it more egregiously, probably because the corporate speech was at least compiled by a human---even if it is not the thoughts of an individual, it is the "thoughts" of an "entity", the abstract corporation, which the writer was speaking for, and so you can still wrap your mind around the fact that it is communicating with you.
children.textZhHtml:
我认为有一种机制，当一个人对你说话时，你可以“镜像”他们的内部心理状态，而写作的质量通常与你从这种心理状态中获得多少快乐或信息或你的目标相对应。重要的是这些词本身只是指向状态的指针。因此，说话的人，如果他们很熟练，会给出足够的词语和足够的多样性，这样你就可以开始自己创造一种与他们相似的状态。

这是 LLM 写作并没有真正做到的事情。由于没有精神状态，无论如何都没有什么可以反映的，并且以某种方式你可以检测到它的缺失，尽管很难用语言表达任何机制。公司演讲也未能以同样的方式激活这一机制，但法学硕士似乎做得更令人震惊，可能是因为公司演讲至少是由人类编译——即使它不是个人的想法，它也是一个“实体”的“想法”，即作者所代表的抽象公司，因此你仍然可以理解它正在与你交流的事实。

children.author: onlyrealcuzzo
children.textRawHtml:
> I am curious why LLM writing has such an uncanny valley feel to it.

Because they are HEAVILY trained to give addictive responses.

They don't want to just answer your question. They want to sycophantically make you feel like a genius for being smart enough to use them.
children.textZhHtml:
> 我很好奇为什么 LLM 写作有如此恐怖谷的感觉。

因为他们大量接受过训练，能够给出令人上瘾的反应。

他们不想只回答你的问题。 他们想让你觉得自己是个天才，因为你足够聪明，可以使用它们。

children.author: snazz
children.textRawHtml: This makes some good intuitive sense, but to me the sycophancy feels like it is an emergent property of turning a next word predictor into a conversational chatbot whether or not it’s intentionally trained that way. Your prompt and its earlier responses is all it has in its context window, so of course it lends undue importance to everything you say. Does that seem like a contributing factor to you?
children.textZhHtml: 这具有很好的直观意义，但对我来说，阿谀奉承感觉像是将下一个单词预测器转变为会话聊天机器人的一种新兴属性，无论它是否是有意这样训练的。您的提示及其之前的响应就是其上下文窗口中的全部内容，因此它当然会过分重视您所说的一切。这对您来说是一个促成因素吗？

children.author: poly2it
children.textRawHtml:
> trained to give addictive responses

I've heard this a lot but I'm not sure it makes sense. Nobody I talk to like Claude's output. In fact, they all loathe it.

Is there a silent majority of Claude users who really enjoy what we call the LLM-isms? Maybe, but isn't Claude also largely aimed at developers?
children.textZhHtml:
> 经过训练可以给出令人上瘾的反应

我听过很多次这样的说法，但我不确定它是否有意义。和我交谈过的人都不喜欢克劳德的作品。事实上，他们都讨厌它。

是否有沉默的大多数 Claude 用户真正喜欢我们所说的 LLM 主义？也许吧，但 Claude 不也是主要针对开发人员吗？

children.author: logicallee
children.textRawHtml:
>Is there a silent majority of Claude users who really enjoy what we call the LLM-isms? Maybe, but isn't Claude also largely aimed at developers?

Purely out of my own curiosity, I just asked Claude to have fun with itself by making itself a game it enjoys, to play it, and to write its experience.[1] I don't know if it's true or confabulated (maybe it doesn't really know its experience and is just hallucinating it) but I didn't mind reading it, the prose is fine for me. I don't mind reading Claude's writing. I mean let's be honest, we all read Claude's writing all day, most of the submissions on the front page on any given day are written by Claude.

Just before I made that game, I had Fable write up a scholarly report on any subject[2], it chose introspection by LLM's. (This is what made me think of asking it to play a game.) I didn't mind reading it, even though I don't think it really added anything very interesting. I don't think what it wrote is worth publishing, but I read it with interest.

I found I could read it easily and get up to date on the state of this question that it picked to answer.

So the bottom line is I don't mind reading Claude's output that much. Of course, I'm annoyed every time it says "honest", "genuine", "load-bearing", whenever it pushes back gently against something, etc. But it's not the end of the world.

[1] https://github.com/robss2020/claude-fable-5-having-fun

[2] https://claude.ai/share/f0122611-22c0-43a5-ab4a-d6863167bdd6
children.textZhHtml:
>是否有沉默的大多数克劳德用户真正喜欢我们所谓的法学硕士主义？也许吧，但Claude不也是主要针对开发者吗？

纯粹出于我自己的好奇心，我只是让Claude玩得开心，让自己成为一个自己喜欢的游戏，玩它，写它的经验。[1]我不知道这是真的还是杜撰的（也许它并不真正知道它的经历，只是产生了幻觉）但我不介意读它，散文对我来说很好。我不介意读克劳德的作品。 我的意思是说实话，我们整天都在读 Claude 的文章，任何一天首页上的大部分提交内容都是 Claude 写的。

就在我制作那个游戏之前，我让《神鬼寓言》写了一份关于任何主题的学术报告[2]，它选择了法学硕士的反思。 （这就是让我想到要求它玩游戏的原因。）我不介意阅读它，尽管我认为它并没有真正添加任何非常有趣的东西。 我认为它写的内容不值得发表，但我饶有兴趣地阅读了它。

我发现我可以轻松阅读它并了解它选择回答的这个问题的最新状态。

所以底线是我不介意阅读克劳德的输出那么多。当然，每次它说“诚实”、“真诚”、“承重”，每当它轻轻地推回某物等等，我都会很恼火。但这不是世界末日。

[1] https://github.com/robss2020/claude-fable-5-having-fun

[2] https://claude.ai/share/f0122611-22c0-43a5-ab4a-d6863167bdd6
